state.final_answer: Clinical problem representation: A patient with a two‑year progressive spastic paraplegia, sensory level at T3‑T4, and urinary incontinence, previously labeled multiple sclerosis or myelitis, shows punctate brain white‑matter lesions sparing the corpus callosum and a symmetric long‑segment ring‑like spinal cord lesion with normal CSF cellularity, IgG index and absent oligoclonal bands. Prioritized diagnostic categories include aquaporin‑4 IgG‑positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein IgG‑associated disease, and primary progressive multiple sclerosis. Next investigations to distinguish them include serum AQP4‑IgG and MOG‑IgG cell‑based assays, contrast‑enhanced spinal MRI to assess enhancement pattern, visual evoked potentials and optical coherence tomography for optic nerve involvement, serum vitamin B12, copper, and infectious screen (HIV, syphilis), and consideration of spinal cord biopsy if seronegative. The brain MRI distribution lacking periventricular and callosal lesions and the spinal ring‑like pattern argue against typical MS and favor NMOSD or MOGAD, while the normal CSF and negative oligoclonal bands further reduce the likelihood of MS but do not exclude it because a minority of MS patients are OCB‑negative and NMOSD can have normal CSF. Therefore imaging and CSF shift probability toward NMOSD/MOGAD but cannot definitively confirm either without antibody testing.
